What is meant by the term 'Height of Tide'?

The vertical distance between the Chart Datum and the water level.
The distance between the seabed and the surface.
The difference between Mean High Water and Mean Low Water.
bank.explanation: The 'Height of Tide' is the vertical distance between the water surface and Chart Datum at any given time.

bank.explanation: Isobar lines connect points of equal atmospheric pressure, helping to identify systems like depressions or anticyclones.

options: When the moon is at its first or last quarter
When the moon is at perigee (closest to Earth)
Around the time of a New or Full moon
Only during the autumnal equinox
bank.question: When do 'Spring' tides typically occur?
What is the primary purpose of a 'Safe Water Mark'?
options: To mark the start of a preferred channel to Starboard
To indicate that there is navigable water all around the mark
To mark a specific underwater hazard like a wreck
To denote the boundary of a restricted military zone
bank.explanation: A safe water mark (red and white stripes) indicates that there is navigable water all around the position.

bank.question: What day shape must a power-driven vessel 'constrained by her draught' exhibit?
options: A cylinder
Three shapes in a vertical line (ball-diamond-ball)
A single black ball
Two cones with apexes together (hourglass)
bank.explanation: The 'Vessel Constrained by her Draught' day shape is a cylinder, as per COLREG Rule 27.

bank.question: On a Part 1 or SSR registered UK vessel, where should the 'Port of Registry' be displayed?
bank.explanation: The Transom (stern) of the boat is the standard location for the vessel's name and its port of registry.

bank.question: In tidal theory, how is the 'Time of High Water' at a Secondary Port usually calculated?
options: Multiply the Standard Port height by the time difference
Standard Port height plus/minus the specific 'Chart Datum' offset
Standard Port data adjusted by time and height differences from the tide tables
Directly using the nearest port's tidal curve without adjustments
bank.explanation: Secondary port calculations use the time and height differences provided in the tide tables relative to a linked Standard Port.

bank.question: What are the night-time lights for a vessel 'Not Under Command' (NUC)?
options: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
Two all-round green lights in a vertical line
One red light over one white light
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Not Under Command' displays two all-round red lights in a vertical line when under way.

bank.question: In coastal navigation, what is a 'Transit' (or Range)?

A bearing taken from a single lighthouse using a compass
A line of position formed by the alignment of two charted fixed objects
The path a vessel takes when corrected for tidal stream

Anticlockwise and inwards towards the centre
bank.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, what is the wind direction and circulation pattern around an area of High Pressure?
bank.explanation: High-pressure systems (anticyclones) in the Northern Hemisphere circulate air in a clockwise direction.
A Starboard Hand lateral mark in IALA Region A is green and, if it has a topmark, it is a single green cone (triangle).

options: Charted Depth + Height of Tide
Charted Depth - Height of Tide
Drying Height + Height of Tide
Chart Datum + Draught of the vessel

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what is the minimum light requirement for a power-driven vessel of less than 7 metres in length whose maximum speed does not exceed 7 knots?
options: Standard sidelights and a steaming light
A single strobe light and a whistle
A single all-round white light and sidelights (if practicable)
No lights are required if staying within 1 mile of the coast
bank.explanation: A vessel under 7 metres with a maximum speed of 7 knots may exhibit a single all-round white light and sidelights if practicable.

bank.explanation: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves over a colder sea surface, common in the UK during spring and early summer.

An increase in wind speed according to the Beaufort scale
A shift in wind direction caused by a tall headland
